quizName: DMV Practice Test #13 25 Questions • Passing Score 20

questions.question: Studies show that most riders in crashes:

options.text: Do not brake the front tire enough and brake the rear tire too much.
Brake the front tire too much and do not brake the rear tire enough.
Only use the front brake.
Only use the rear brake.

questions.correctAnswerText: Do not brake the front tire enough and brake the rear tire too much.
questions.explanation: Most riders in crashes do not brake the front tire enough and brake the rear tire too much.

questions.question: When braking, you should:

options.text: Apply the front brake first, then the rear.
Apply the rear brake first, then the front.
Use both brakes at the same time.
Use the brakes in any order.

questions.correctAnswerText: Use both brakes at the same time.
questions.explanation: Use both brakes at the same time whenever you slow down or stop.

questions.question: When another vehicle passes you from behind, you should:

options.text: Move onto the shoulder.
Stay in the left portion of your lane.
Stay in the center portion of your lane.
Stay in the right portion of your lane.

questions.correctAnswerText: Stay in the center portion of your lane.
questions.explanation: When being passed, stay in the center portion of your lane. This is the safest position. Riding on the side closest to the passing vehicle can cause a collision. Riding on the far side may encourage the other driver to return to your lane before it is safe.

questions.question: It is most important to flash your brake light when:

options.text: You are passing another vehicle.
You need to slow down suddenly.
There is a stop sign ahead.
Your signals do not work.

questions.correctAnswerText: You need to slow down suddenly.
questions.explanation: A motorcycle has only one brake light, which is not as visible as the two larger brake lights on cars and trucks. Flashing your brake light helps alert other drivers, especially when you slow down faster than expected.

questions.question: A proper lane position should do all of the following, except:

options.text: Help you set up for turns.
Give you an escape route.
Help you avoid wind blasts from other vehicles.
Place you in another vehicle's blind spot.

questions.correctAnswerText: Place you in another vehicle's blind spot.
questions.explanation: A good lane position helps you see others and be seen. It helps you avoid wind blasts, blind spots, and road hazards. It also discourages other drivers from sharing your lane and gives you an escape route if needed.

questions.question: As weight shifts to the front of your motorcycle while braking, you should:

options.text: Slowly increase pressure on the front brake.
Use more rear brake pressure.
Not worry about it. Weight transfer does not affect your motorcycle.
Try to lock the front tire.

questions.correctAnswerText: Slowly increase pressure on the front brake.
questions.explanation: As your motorcycle's weight shifts forward during braking, slowly increase the pressure you apply to the front brake lever.

questions.question: Most motorcycles have curved, or convex, mirrors. These mirrors:

options.text: Are easy to get used to right away.
Make cars look closer than they really are.
Show a narrow view of the road.
Make cars look farther away than they really are.

questions.correctAnswerText: Make cars look farther away than they really are.
questions.explanation: Curved mirrors show more of the road behind you than flat mirrors do. However, they make objects appear farther away than they actually are. Practice judging distances in curved mirrors if you are not used to them.

questions.question: Hearing protection is:

options.text: Not needed if you wear a helmet.
Needed in addition to a helmet.
Only needed on windy days.
Not needed if you are carrying a passenger.

questions.correctAnswerText: Needed in addition to a helmet.
questions.explanation: Engine and wind noise can damage your hearing, even with a helmet. Hearing protection guards against this while still letting you hear important sounds like horns and sirens.

questions.question: If you accidentally lock your rear wheel while braking on a road with good traction, you should:

options.text: Keep it locked until you stop completely.
Release the rear brake and use only the front brake.
Release the rear brake, then apply it again quickly.
Release the rear brake and shift to a lower gear.

questions.correctAnswerText: Keep it locked until you stop completely.
questions.explanation: If you accidentally lock the rear brake on a road with good traction, keep it locked until you stop. Your motorcycle should still be controllable if it is upright and going straight.

questions.question: How can you discourage another vehicle from sharing your lane?

options.text: Ride in the middle of your lane.
Ride in the left portion of your lane.
Ride in the right portion of your lane.
Swerve from side to side in your lane.

questions.correctAnswerText: Ride in the middle of your lane.
questions.explanation: To discourage other drivers from trying to share your lane, ride in the center portion of the lane.

questions.question: Which of the following does NOT affect blood alcohol content (BAC)?

options.text: The amount of alcohol consumed
How fast the alcohol is consumed
The drinker's body weight
How often the drinker consumes alcohol

questions.correctAnswerText: How often the drinker consumes alcohol
questions.explanation: Three main factors affect BAC: the amount of alcohol consumed, how fast it is consumed, and the drinker's body weight. Drinking and driving is illegal and dangerous.

questions.question: The best protection for a motorcycle operator is:

options.text: Keeping distance between your vehicle and other vehicles.
A good leather jacket.
Sturdy boots.
A good understanding of motorcycle laws.

questions.correctAnswerText: Keeping distance between your vehicle and other vehicles.
questions.explanation: Distance is your best protection against crashes. Keep plenty of space between you and other vehicles so you have time to react to other drivers' mistakes. Wearing proper gear is also important.

questions.question: The center of a lane:

options.text: Is always the best part of the lane for a motorcycle.
Often has oil and grease, but is usually safe for riding.
Often has oil and grease, and is never safe for riding.
Is the smoothest part of the lane.

questions.correctAnswerText: Often has oil and grease, but is usually safe for riding.
questions.explanation: Oil from cars collects in the center of each lane. On dry roads, this area usually has enough grip for safe riding. Avoid riding on heavy oil buildup, often found at busy intersections or toll booths.

questions.question: When going through a curve, you should:

options.text: Always stay in the same part of the lane throughout the curve.
Always stay in the left part of the lane throughout the curve.
Always stay in the right part of the lane throughout the curve.
Remember that the best path may not follow the road's curve.

questions.correctAnswerText: Remember that the best path may not follow the road's curve.
questions.explanation: Road and traffic conditions change. Be ready to adjust your lane position as needed. The best path through a curve does not always follow the road's curve.

questions.question: Your lane position should do all of the following, EXCEPT:

options.text: Increase your ability to see and be seen.
Avoid other drivers' blind spots.
Avoid surface hazards.
Block access to an escape route.

questions.correctAnswerText: Block access to an escape route.
questions.explanation: Good lane position increases your visibility, helps you avoid blind spots and surface hazards, and discourages other drivers from sharing your lane. It should give you an escape route if danger appears.

questions.question: If you must brake and swerve to avoid a hazard, you should:

options.text: Do one action, then the other.
Do both at the same time.
Always brake first, then swerve.
Try to use only the brakes.

questions.correctAnswerText: Do one action, then the other.
questions.explanation: Brake and swerve separately, not at the same time. You can brake then swerve, or swerve then brake.

questions.question: When preparing to pass on the left, ride on the left side of your lane because:

options.text: The right side could be slippery.
It gives you the best view of hazards in the next lane.
People don't usually expect to be passed on their left.
It places you in the car's rearview mirror.

questions.correctAnswerText: It gives you the best view of hazards in the next lane.
questions.explanation: Riding in the left part of your lane when preparing to pass improves your sight line and makes you more visible to oncoming traffic.

questions.question: If you brake while in a curve:

options.text: Only use the front brake.
It will be the same as braking on a straight road.
You will have more grip as you lean into the curve.
You may have less grip as you lean into the curve.

questions.correctAnswerText: You may have less grip as you lean into the curve.
questions.explanation: You can use both brakes while turning, but you must be careful. Some tire grip is used for turning while leaning, so less grip is available for braking.

questions.question: When braking on a slippery surface, you should:

options.text: Use both the front and rear brakes.
Use quick, hard pressure on the front brake to prevent the front tire from locking.
Only use the rear brake.
Use one brake only.

questions.correctAnswerText: Use both the front and rear brakes.
questions.explanation: On slippery surfaces, use both brakes to slow down. Squeeze the brake lever gradually to prevent the front wheel from locking, and apply gentle pressure to the rear brake.

questions.question: What does this signal mean?

options.text: Follow me
Slow down
Speed up
Exit

questions.correctAnswerText: Follow me
questions.explanation: Hand signals are used to communicate when riding in groups. This signal means "follow me."

questions.question: Motorcycle headlights are:

options.text: Usually stronger than car headlights.
Usually as strong as car headlights.
Usually weaker than car headlights.
Usually bigger than car headlights.

questions.correctAnswerText: Usually weaker than car headlights.
questions.explanation: Motorcycle headlights are smaller and weaker than car headlights.

questions.question: Riders wearing helmets are ________ more likely to survive a crash than riders without helmets.

options.text: Two times
Three times
Eight times
Ten times

questions.correctAnswerText: Three times
questions.explanation: A helmet makes you three times more likely to survive a head injury in a crash at any speed.

questions.question: When riding at night you should:

options.text: Speed up.
Follow cars more closely.
Use the headlights of cars ahead to see the road.
Wear dark glasses.

questions.correctAnswerText: Use the headlights of cars ahead to see the road.
questions.explanation: At night, slow down and increase your following distance. Use the headlights of vehicles ahead to see farther down the road. Stay flexible with your lane position.

questions.question: Without a helmet, a motorcycle rider is ________ more likely to suffer a critical head injury in a crash.

options.text: Three times
Four times
Five times
Six times

questions.correctAnswerText: Five times
questions.explanation: Without a helmet, a rider is five times more likely to suffer a critical head injury in a crash.

questions.question: To work well, an eye or face shield must:

options.text: Attach securely.
Block all air from passing through.
Not allow eyeglasses to fit underneath.
Block your side vision.

questions.correctAnswerText: Attach securely.
questions.explanation: A good eye or face shield must have no scratches, resist damage, allow clear views to the sides, attach securely, let air pass through to stop fogging, and fit over eyeglasses if needed.
